passages.title: The Lighthouse at Eddystone
passages.subtitle: Four towers on one rock
passages.instruction: This is a fixture, not a real exam paper. It exercises every question type the builder supports so that the admin importer, the student runner and the grader can be checked end to end.

blocks.label: A
blocks.content: The Eddystone rocks lie fourteen kilometres off the coast of Plymouth, submerged at high water and directly across the approach to one of England's busiest harbours. Four lighthouses have stood there in succession, and the story of the four is, in miniature, the story of how engineers learned to build in the sea.

blocks.label: B
blocks.content: The first, completed by Henry Winstanley in 1698, was a timber structure elaborately ornamented with iron scrollwork and open galleries. Winstanley was so confident of it that he expressed a wish to be inside during the greatest storm that ever blew. In November 1703 he was, and neither he nor the tower was seen again.

blocks.label: C
blocks.content: John Smeaton's tower of 1759 was the decisive advance. He shaped it like the trunk of an oak, broad at the base and tapering upwards, and he cut the granite blocks with dovetails so that each course locked into its neighbours and into the rock itself. He also revived hydraulic lime, a mortar that sets under water. The tower stood for one hundred and twenty-three years and was dismantled only because the rock beneath it, not the masonry, had begun to fail.

blocks.label: D
blocks.content: James Douglass replaced it in 1882 with the tower that stands today, seating it on a cylindrical base designed to break up the waves before they reached the shaft. Smeaton's tower was taken down course by course and rebuilt on Plymouth Hoe, where it remains open to visitors.
